newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Clinton tells Romanians to press on for NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Clinton tells Romanians to press on for NATO entry.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday told tens of thousands of cheering Romanians, apparently unbowed by the country's failure to win early NATO membership, to press ahead with reform to win entry next time.

Addressing the crowd in University Square, where dozens of young people died in the 1989 revolt that toppled communism, Clinton said Romania was "one of the strongest candidates" for inclusion when enlargement is re-examined in two years' time.

"I know that Romania would have liked to be among the first of Europe's new democracies to join NATO," Clinton told the crowd cheering "Clinton, Clinton!" and "NATO, NATO!" in brilliant late afternoon sunshine.

"I welcome Romania's deep desire to contribute even more fully to Europe's security and strength. I want that too -- for Europe, America and you -- and I say to you today: Stay the course and Romania will cross the milestone."
The U.S. president later left for Denmark, where he was due to make a brief visit before returning to Washington.
On a tour of Bucharest's Village Museum, which groups traditional houses from throughout the country of 22 million, he told reporters he had been overwhelmed by the reception.
"It was amazing. I knew they were very friendly toward America," he said. "Keep in mind that they have suffered more than others under communism."

Clinton's enthusiastic reception in the streets crowned an eight-hour stop in Romania three days after a NATO summit in Madrid kept Romania out of the Alliance's first eastward expansion along with the former Yugoslav republic of Slovenia.
At American insistence, only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic were invited to start talks on joining. Romania and Slovenia were named as prime candidates for future expansion.
Clinton, the first U.S. leader to visit Romania in 22 years, said that as long as Romania pursued change "America will be by your side."
"The door to NATO is open. It will stay open. And we will help you walk through it," he said. "NATO is committed to review aspiring members in 1999 and Romania is one of the strongest candidates."

Clinton also applauded efforts to mend fences with Romania's neighbours Hungary and Ukraine and the inclusion in the government of representatives of the country's 1.4 million-strong Hungarian minority.

The crowd was far more numerous and enthusiastic than a gathering a day earlier in Warsaw's Castle Square, where Clinton said the newly expanded NATO would end the divisions which rent Europe after the close of World War Two.
Clinton had earlier urged Romanian President Emil Constantinescu to press on with reforms to persuade the West that change was there to stay.
He also told Romanian political figures the country was "a beacon of hope in a region that has seen so much conflict", a reference to turmoil in neighbouring former Yugoslavia.

Constantinescu told the gathering in University Square the Madrid summit had "declared Romania as a privileged partner for the second wave of its expansion provided the economic and political reforms continue".
He told the crowd: "We are not going to stop because the vast majority of the Romanian people want to live in a stable and prosperous country."

As he approached the rostrum, Clinton stood head bowed near several white stone crosses marking the spot where protesters were shot dead scant days before Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was executed in December 1989.
After the address, he was handed a Romanian blue yellow and red tricolour with the centre ripped out -- symbol of the revolt during which the communist crest was torn from flags.
In addition to its NATO aspirations, Romania wants a "strategic partnership" with Washington. Clinton said Washington fully backed the concept "because Romania is important to America".
